extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, congressional staff, patent practitioners, industry stakeholders and patent policy advocates
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing proposed changes to U.S. patent law (e.g., H.R. 1249/America Invents Act) for effects on litigation, PTO operations, patent quality, constitutional compliance, and small/inventor protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expand low-cost alternatives to litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent reform legislation should seek to expand opportunities for low-cost, efficient alternatives to litigation as a way of resolving disputes about the validity of issued patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inter partes reexamination (and similar procedures) should be preserved or enhanced rather than constrained; reforms should make administrative review a viable, efficient alternative to district-court litigation for weeding out bad patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid arbitrary early filing deadlines for inter partes review
rubrics_metrics.description: H.R. 1249 sets a 12-month deadline for a defendant in litigation to file a petition for inter partes review starting from service of the complaint; the 12-month period is arbitrary and fails to account for complex cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deadlines should be tied to substantive progress in litigation (example: entry of a district-court order construing the relevant patent claims) to give defendants sufficient time to prepare legitimate petitions in complex multi-patent, multi-defendant cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a permissive institution threshold for inter partes reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill raises the initiation threshold to where the Director must find 'a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail with respect to at least one of the claims challenged in the petition.' The existing standard asks whether a petition raises a 'substantial new question of patentability.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve the existing 'substantial new question of patentability' standard because (as noted) the majority of inter partes reexaminations initiated under the current standard have been ultimately deemed meritorious; a stricter/unclear standard risks rejecting legitimate petitions at the outset without sufficient inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect and dedicate PTO user fees to PTO operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 22 would ensure that fees collected by the PTO fund the office and its administration; fee diversion by Congress has hampered PTO efforts to hire/retain examiners and implement necessary technological improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide PTO with full access to the user fees it collects (prevent fee diversion) as a step toward reducing application backlog and improving patent quality; allow Director to adjust fees with appropriate congressional oversight to enable staffing and tech improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt first-inventor-to-file while preserving key protections
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill shifts the U.S. to a first-inventor-to-file system intended to end interference proceedings; supporters argue it is constitutional and returns to earlier U.S. practice similar to first-to-register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If moving to first-inventor-to-file, retain protections such as a 1-year grace period, protections for universities (e.g., CREATE Act), robust prior-user-rights, and measures to prevent disadvantaging independent inventors; ensure statutory language still requires the applicant to be an actual inventor (first-inventor-to-file, not 'first-to-file' without inventorship).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve and strengthen prior user rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 5 would create a prior user right for those who first commercially use inventions, protecting early inventors and manufacturers (while purportedly protecting universities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior user rights should be robust and include protection during the statutory grace period; such protections should encompass non-disclosure forms of prior art (e.g., trade-secret uses) so that commercially first users are not unfairly displaced by later filers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reform false patent marking to deter frivolous suits while preserving actual-harm claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 16 would put an end to frivolous false patent marking cases, while still preserving the right of those who suffered actual harm to bring actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance deterring opportunistic/fee-driven false marking litigation with preserving remedies for parties that have actually been harmed by false marking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict joinder of tenuously-related defendants
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 19 restricts joinder of defendants who have tenuous connections to underlying patent disputes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit permissive joinder so plaintiffs cannot lump together many defendants with weak connections to force settlements or inflate litigation costs; tailor joinder rules to reflect meaningful joint liability or coordinated conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pilot program to use PTO expertise in court review of business-method patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 18 provides for a tailored pilot program allowing PTO experts to help the court review the validity of certain business-method patents using the best available prior art as an alternative to costly litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use PTO technical expertise and superior prior-art resources in a limited pilot to provide courts with better prior-art information and reduce costly back-end litigation; program should be narrowly tailored and evaluated for effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure adequate PTO resources to reduce backlog and improve patent quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTO faces a massive backlog of pending applications and needs resources to hire/retain qualified examiners and implement technological improvements; inadequate funding harms inventors and small businesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation should enable the PTO to access and use its collected fees to hire examiners, upgrade systems, and shorten pendency (current backlog cited as ~1.2 million and pendency ~3 years), thereby improving front-end examination quality and reducing downstream litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve constitutional protections for inventors (first-inventor vs. first-to-file concerns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Opponents argue the bill violates Article I, Section 8 and the Fifth Amendment by denying the actual first inventor patent rights simply because another party filed first; proponents argue first-inventor-to-file is constitutional and consistent with Congressional authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any reform must be evaluated against constitutional history, precedent, and legal opinion to ensure that changes do not inappropriately strip inventors of rights or effect an unconstitutional taking; statutory definitions and dispute-resolution mechanisms should respect inventorship and established constitutional principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain protections that benefit small inventors and universities
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisions such as a 1-year grace period, CREATE Act treatment of collaborative research, a permanent small-business ombudsman, and fee reductions for small entities are cited as necessary protections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include or preserve statutory provisions that protect small inventors and universities from being disadvantaged by procedural changes (grace periods, CREATE Act exceptions, permanent ombudsman, targeted fee relief) to ensure access and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess fiscal impacts and avoid harmful fee diversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns were raised that removing protections for patent fees and allowing fee diversion increases the deficit and undermines PTO functioning (examples: diversion of $85-100M despite existing prohibitions; projected budget impacts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy evaluations should include fiscal analysis of fee diversion, compliance with budget rules (e.g., CutGo concerns), and ensure fee-policy changes do not unintentionally worsen PTO funding or the federal deficit.
